lines.speaker: Earl Funk

lines.text: I'd like to call this meeting to order. At this time, I'd like to, uh, give the opening to Councillor Michael Zwaagstra.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. Back in the 1990s, I joined the Columbia House Music Club. By signing up, I agreed to buy several CDs at full price. In return, I received a bunch of free CDs. It seemed like a good idea at the time. I got even more free CDs when I convinced other people to sign up. However, there was a catch. Every month, Columbia House would send me an unsolicited CD. Unless I remembered to send it back, at my own expense, by a specific date, I would be billed the full cost. It was a classic example of negative option billing, where you are assumed to have bought the product unless you proactively decline it. This was how Columbia House and other similar clubs made their money. They knew that plenty of customers would forget to send back their CDs. Let's just say that I terminated my membership at the earliest opportunity, and so did many others after they realized what they had signed up for. Most people strongly dislike negative option billing, and for very good reason. By putting the onus on customers to opt out, there ends up being a lot of accidental purchases. This might be great for the company, but it's terrible for consumers. Negative option billing was bad enough with CDs. Now picture it being used in end-of-life medical care. In 2016, The Canadian government legalized assisted suicide, now known by the euphemism MAID, for people whose death was reasonably foreseeable. However, it didn't take long to expand MAID's eligibility to the point where MAID is now one of the most easily accessible medical procedures in Canada. By spring of next year, even people whose sole underlying medical condition is mental illness will become eligible for MAID. Some medical practitioners aren't even waiting until next year to offer this procedure to mentally ill patients. For example, on June 2nd of this year, Catherine Mentler went to the Vancouver General Hospital suffering from a mental health crisis. To her shock, the clinician asked Mentler whether she had ever considered MAiD. The clinician then went on to describe MAiD as a more comfortable process than dying by a drug overdose. Incredibly, when this story hit the media, the Vancouver Health Authority did not deny that the conversation took place. Rather, it claimed that the MAiD discussion was simply a tool used by the clinician to assess the risk of self-harm. However, this so-called tool apparently didn't work very well since Mentler left the hospital in greater distress than when she had arrived. Sadly, this is not the only time that this sort of thing has happened. We all remember last year when we heard about a number of veterans being encouraged to try MAiD after they asked Veterans Affairs Canada for support. It's shocking that anyone would think that this was an acceptable way to treat our veterans. Given how quickly the eligibility criteria for MAiD are being expanded and how comfortable some medical professionals are bringing it up with patients, it becomes entirely plausible that MAiD will eventually be routinely offered to everyone. I shudder to think about the conversations that might someday take place in some personal care homes. Will we reach the point as a society where MAiD happens by default unless we specifically opt out? I certainly hope not. But then, few people thought that MAiD would become as widely available as it already is right now. The current trend does not bode well for the future. Negative option billing was a lousy way to sell CDs, and it's an even worse way to provide end-of-life medical care. Life, not death, should always be the default option. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Daniel Banman

lines.label: Daniel Banman (Delegation, Robert D. and Joanne S. Banman Heritage Foundation)
lines.text: Fantastic. Uh, good evening, Mayor and councillors. My name is Daniel Banman. I'm a representative of the Robert D. and Joanne S. Banman Heritage Foundation. Uh, our foundation was established in 2008 to recognize Steinbach's history The foundation was involved in projects such as the Millennium Clock Tower and the large mural depicting Reimer Avenue in the '50s. I'm here to introduce the latest project, which is a statue commemorating the Ruslander migration of Mennonites to the Steinbach region between 1923 and 1926. My great-grandparents, Jacob and Barbara Bandmann, were part of the Ruslander migration. They arrived in 1924 and 1926 respectively. Thank you. My grandfather was aboard the vessel, the Empress of Scotland. He arrived in Montreal on the 2nd of October, 1926, at 8 years of age, along with his mother, father, 3 sisters, and his brother. Being the 100th anniversary of the migration to our community, we thought it would be an ideal time to commemorate this key part of our local history. We hope the statue will also pay tribute to all the people who have had to flee their home countries and settle in our region over the years. It's important to recognize that exactly 100 years ago after the Ruslander migration, people are also escaping the same region to Steinbach under the exact same circumstances. The statue itself is bronze and it's 9 feet tall. It weighs around 1,800 pounds and it depicts a young family that was forced to flee their homeland. The statue will be located in front of the Millennium Clock Tower as seen in our scale mockup. We hope to have the statue in place by October this year, at which we plan to have a formal dedication ceremony. I'm happy to answer any questions you have about the project, and I'd like to thank you for your time.

And I think this will— this is a great thing for our Main Street. It's a great piece of art to have downtown. Thank you.
